content: The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation (CFF) is a non-profit organization based in the United States that was established with the mission of curing and controlling cystic fibrosis. The Foundation provides comprehensive information about cystic fibrosis (CF) and funds research aimed at improving the quality of life for individuals affected by the disease. Additionally, the Foundation actively participates in legislative advocacy efforts related to cystic fibrosis. The Cystic Fibrosis Foundation was founded in 1955 by a group of volunteers in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Beyond funding research grants and supporting clinical trials for cystic fibrosis, the Foundation accredits and promotes 115 specialized centers dedicated to the treatment of individuals with CF. It also operates over 80 chapters and offices across the United States. In 1989, scientists affiliated with the Foundation identified the gene responsible for cystic fibrosis, a discovery considered pivotal in the pursuit of a cure for the disease. The Foundation has been a leader in CF treatment, playing a significant role in the development and approval of four FDA-approved therapies. In the United States, the Foundation has popularized the use of the registered trademark 65 Roses® as a more accessible alternative to the term cystic fibrosis, which can be challenging to pronounce. According to Foundation lore, the term originated in 1965 when a volunteer, Mary Weiss, heard her four-year-old son, Richard Weiss, pronounce cystic fibrosis as 65 Roses. The term has since been embraced by children to describe their condition and has become closely associated with the Foundation, which uses a rose as its symbol.
